name: Ruscus aculeatus

lead: Ruscus aculeatus, or butcher's broom, is a low Eurasian shrub. Its rhizome extract contains steroidal saponins (ruscogenins) believed to constrict veins and calm inflammation. It is sold as an oral venotonic and appears in creams.

For appearance, people use it in the hope of reducing eye bags and under-eye puffiness through the same vein-tightening and anti-swelling action. Trials have studied leg venous symptoms and swelling, not the eye area.

paras: Users take oral extract (often combined with hesperidin methyl chalcone and vitamin C) or apply products containing it to the under-eye area. Results in studies of leg symptoms are assessed over weeks of regular use.

Poison-centre reports in Italy relate mostly to children eating the berries, according to Wikipedia. Oral use is usually discussed with a clinician, particularly for people on medicines or with diabetes, since one case report linked it to ketoacidosis.

chain: Ruscogenins act on veins and capillaries
angle.text: People apply or take Ruscus extract hoping to lessen swelling and the look of under-eye puffiness. The mechanism is borrowed from leg-vein studies; its use around the eyes is a community and cosmetic idea.

lead: Ruscus aculeatus, butcher's broom, is a low evergreen shrub of Eurasia whose stiff stems were once bundled to clean butchers' chopping blocks. Its rhizome was used traditionally as a diuretic and for swelling.[1] The main compounds are steroidal saponins, especially ruscogenins, described as anti-inflammatory and believed to constrict veins.[1][2]

In looksmaxxing the interest is in depuffing: the theory is that a venotonic could firm vessels and reduce fluid that contributes to eye bags. The research, however, concerns chronic venous disease in the legs, where a standardised Ruscus extract with hesperidin methyl chalcone and vitamin C has been used for decades in some European countries.[3]

A 2017 meta-analysis of 10 randomised placebo-controlled trials (719 patients) found Ruscus-containing venoactive drugs improved seven leg symptoms, including pain, heaviness and the feeling of swelling, versus placebo.[4]
infobox: Ruscus + hesperidin methyl chalcone + vitamin C

paras: The plant is a shrub up to around 80 cm with flat, leaf-like cladodes, small flowers in spring and red berries on female plants.[1] Phytochemical reviews describe the genus as a rich source of bioactive steroidal saponins.[5]

Ruscogenins are believed to constrict veins and reduce inflammation; one proposed mechanism is suppression of leukocyte migration, though Wikipedia says this is not well understood.[1] Pharmacology reviews describe action on veins, capillaries and lymphatics and venoconstriction in the setting of venous hypertension.[2][3]

The 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials found significant improvement in leg pain, heaviness, fatigue, swelling sensation, cramps, itching and paresthesia versus placebo.[4] A 2025 review covers venoactive compounds in chronic venous disease.[6] No studies were found on eye bags or periorbital puffiness.
The Milan Poison Control Centre handled 107 cases from 1995 to 2007, mostly children eating berries, and Wikipedia lists a case report linking butcher's broom to diabetic ketoacidosis.[1]
